lead: Torque, power and brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC) are the numbers a test cell measures to judge every fuel and spark choice the ECU makes. Torque is the twisting effort at the crankshaft. Power is torque multiplied by angular speed. BSFC is the mass of fuel spent for each kilowatt-hour of work delivered at the crankshaft, in g/kWh. Together they show where an engine is strong and where it is economical, and they become the targets stored in the ECU maps.
prereq: You need: the effect of a rich mixture on torque and fuel from engine fuelling and exhaust emissions, and work, power and energy from first-year physics.

blocks.text: Torque T is the twisting effort the crankshaft delivers, in N·m. A dynamometer loads the engine, holds its speed steady and measures T. Turning the shaft through one radian at torque T does T joules of work, so shaft power is T × ω, where ω is the angular speed in rad/s. With speed N in rev/min, ω = 2πN ÷ 60.

blocks.where: P is brake power in W; T is brake torque in N·m; N is speed in rev/min; 2π ÷ 60 converts rev/min to rad/s.

blocks.text: At 3000 rpm and 150 N·m, P = 2π × 3000 × 150 ÷ 60 = 47.1 kW. At 4000 rpm the torque has fallen to 145 N·m, yet P = 60.7 kW. Past the torque peak, speed rises faster than torque falls, so power keeps climbing until torque falls steeply near the top of the speed range.

Brake mean effective pressure (BMEP) lets engines of different sizes be compared. It is the brake work per cycle divided by the total swept volume V<sub>d</sub>. A four-stroke makes one cycle every two revolutions, so the work per cycle is 4πT and BMEP = 4πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub> (for a two-stroke, 2πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub>). With T in N·m and V<sub>d</sub> in m³, BMEP is in Pa; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
A fuel meter gives the fuel mass flow ṁ<sub>f</sub>, usually in kg/h. Dividing it by brake power gives BSFC.

blocks.where: BSFC is in g/kWh; ṁ<sub>f</sub> is in kg/h; P is in kW; 1000 converts kg to g.

blocks.text: A small BSFC is good. A modern petrol engine reaches about 230 to 260 g/kWh at its best point; a diesel reaches about 200 g/kWh or less, because its higher compression ratio and lean running extract more work from each gram. Fuel consumption in kg/h (or L/h) alone cannot compare engines, because it does not say how much work the fuel bought.

One kWh is 3600 kJ. The fuel burnt to make it holds BSFC × CV kJ, where CV is the calorific value in MJ/kg, which is the same number as kJ/g. Their ratio is the brake thermal efficiency η<sub>bth</sub>.

blocks.where: η<sub>bth</sub> is a fraction; BSFC in g/kWh; CV in MJ/kg; 3600 is kJ per kWh.

sections.h3: Mechanical efficiency and the BSFC map

blocks.text: Indicated power is the power the gas delivers to the pistons. Brake power is what is left at the crankshaft after friction and pumping. Friction power = indicated power − brake power, and mechanical efficiency η<sub>m</sub> = brake power ÷ indicated power, about 0.8 to 0.9 for a petrol engine at full load, falling at light load and at high speed.
A BSFC map draws lines of equal BSFC on a chart of speed (x) against torque or BMEP (y). Its lowest-BSFC island sits at moderate speed, about 2000 to 3000 rpm, and fairly high load.

items: At high speed, friction and pumping grow, so more fuel only keeps the engine turning.
At light load, the fixed losses are shared over little brake power, and throttling adds pumping loss, so BSFC is poor.
At full load, the ECU enriches the mixture to protect components, and the extra fuel raises BSFC again.

blocks.text: Measuring torque, power, BSFC and emissions at every speed and load on a test bed is called engine mapping. The ECU fuel and spark tables are filled from these maps (see concept of electronic engine control).

examples.question: A four-cylinder 1.6 L petrol engine runs at 3000 rev/min and 150 N·m. Fuel flow is 11.5 kg/h; petrol CV is 43 MJ/kg. Mechanical efficiency is 0.85. Find the brake power, BMEP, BSFC, brake thermal efficiency, indicated power and friction power.
steps: Indicated power = 47.12 ÷ 0.85 = 55.44 kW; friction power = 55.44 − 47.12 = 8.32 kW.
examples.answer: Brake power 47.12 kW, BMEP 11.78 bar, BSFC 244.04 g/kWh, brake thermal efficiency 34.31 %, indicated power 55.44 kW and friction power 8.32 kW.
examples.check:
import math
P = 2*math.pi*3000*150/60/1000
print(round(P, 2))
print(round(4*math.pi*150/0.0016/1e5, 2))
b = 11.5*1000/P
print(round(b, 2))
print(round(3600/(b*43)*100, 2))
print(round(P/0.85, 2)); print(round(P/0.85 - P, 2))

traps: Putting rev/min straight into P = Tω; convert first with ω = 2πN ÷ 60.
Forgetting the 1000 in BSFC: kg/h ÷ kW gives kg/kWh, a number 1000 times smaller than g/kWh.
Taking BMEP = T ÷ V<sub>d</sub>. For a four-stroke it is 4πT ÷ V<sub>d</sub>; leaving out 4π gives a value about 12.6 times too small.
Confusing the torque peak with the power peak; power peaks at a higher speed.
Using CV in kJ/kg in η = 3600 ÷ (BSFC × CV); it must be in MJ/kg (= kJ/g).

quiz.q: Define BSFC and give its unit.
quiz.a: Fuel mass flow divided by brake power: the fuel used per kWh of crankshaft work, in g/kWh.

quiz.q: Write the relation between brake power, torque and speed, naming every symbol and unit.
quiz.a: P = 2πNT ÷ 60, with P in W, T in N·m and N in rev/min.

quiz.q: Torque peaks at 3000 rpm but power peaks near 6000 rpm. Explain why.
quiz.a: Power = torque × speed. Past the torque peak, speed rises faster than torque falls, so the product keeps growing until torque falls steeply.

quiz.q: An engine holds 130 N·m at 2500 rev/min. Find the brake power.
A diesel uses 9 kg/h of fuel while delivering 40 kW. CV is 43 MJ/kg. Find BSFC and brake thermal efficiency.
Why does the lowest-BSFC island sit at moderate speed and fairly high load rather than at maximum speed or full throttle?
quiz.a: At high speed friction and pumping grow; at light load the fixed losses and throttling are large compared with the small brake power; at full load enrichment adds fuel for little extra work.

quiz.q: Brake power is 60 kW and mechanical efficiency is 0.85. Find indicated power and friction power.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the BSFC map is stored as ECU breakpoint tables of speed against load, and calibration engineers move the breakpoints to cover the driving cycle. Hybrid controllers keep the engine inside its low-BSFC island and let the battery cover peaks. Search next for "BSFC map", "engine mapping dynamometer" and "Willans line".
